questions.stem: Rachel, 34, is 36+2 weeks with a previous term stillbirth. Her CTG and ultrasound are normal and she is going home from the maternity day assessment unit. She asks what she should do if the baby seems quieter again. Which safety-netting advice is best?
options: Do a kick count after a meal and call if you feel fewer than 10 movements in 2 hours
Contact the maternity unit and come in straight away, at any time of day or night
Lie on your left side with a cold drink for an hour, then call if it's no better
Check the heartbeat with a home Doppler first, then decide whether to come in
questions.why: Any reduction or change in her baby's usual pattern of movements should prompt immediate contact and assessment, day or night. She is never wasting anyone's time. This is the core message of the Safer Baby Bundle and RANZCOG guidance.
notes: There is no validated fixed kick count. Women should know their own baby's pattern and report any change, without waiting to reach a number.
Trying a cold drink or a position change delays assessment. Rachel already waited 18 hours doing this, and delay is linked to stillbirth.
Home Dopplers give false reassurance, because a heartbeat can be found even when a baby is compromised. Their use is discouraged.

questions.stem: Rachel, 34, at 36+2 weeks, has had reduced movements for about 18 hours. Her 40-minute CTG is normal, BP is 116/72 and the dipstick is clear. Her last growth scan was at 32 weeks. She had a previous term stillbirth with a small placenta. What is the most appropriate next investigation today?
options: Kleihauer test on maternal blood today to look for fetomaternal haemorrhage
Repeat CTG in one week at her routine antenatal visit
Ultrasound for fetal growth, liquor volume and umbilical artery Doppler
Serum sFlt-1/PlGF ratio to assess for placental dysfunction
questions.why: A normal CTG is only a snapshot. With risk factors for placental insufficiency, reduced fetal movements need an ultrasound the same day to assess fetal growth, amniotic fluid volume and umbilical artery Doppler before she is discharged.
notes: A Kleihauer test looks for fetomaternal haemorrhage after trauma or bleeding. Rachel has had neither, and the test does not assess growth.
Waiting a week leaves possible growth restriction unassessed in a high-risk pregnancy where movements have already reduced.
The sFlt-1/PlGF ratio helps rule out pre-eclampsia when it is suspected. Rachel has no features of it, and the ratio does not measure fetal growth or liquor.

questions.stem: Rachel, 34, at 36+2 weeks, says she often falls asleep or wakes on her back. You advise her to go to sleep on her side. In the third trimester, what is the main mechanism by which going to sleep on the back raises the risk of stillbirth?
options: The uterus compresses the IVC and aorta, reducing venous return and uterine blood flow
The uterus presses the umbilical cord against the maternal lumbar spine for long spells
Splinting of the diaphragm causes maternal hypoxaemia and so fetal hypoxia
Lying supine triggers uterine contractions that cut placental perfusion
questions.why: Lying supine lets the gravid uterus compress the inferior vena cava and aorta. This lowers maternal cardiac output and uteroplacental perfusion, which reduces fetal oxygenation. That is why side sleeping from 28 weeks is advised.
notes: The cord lies inside the amniotic sac, cushioned by liquor. Supine risk comes from compression of the maternal great vessels, not the cord.
Lung volumes fall slightly when supine, but maternal oxygen saturation stays normal. Reduced uterine blood flow is the key mechanism.
Lying supine does not provoke contractions. The harm comes from lower maternal cardiac output and less flow to the uterus.

questions.stem: You palpate Rachel's abdomen at 36+2 weeks. The baby is in a longitudinal lie and cephalic presentation, with the fetal back on her left side. Where should you place the hand-held Doppler to find the fetal heart most easily?
options: Midline at the uterine fundus, just below the xiphisternum, with gentle pressure
Above the umbilicus on the mother's right side
Midline just above the pubic symphysis, over the fetal head
Below the umbilicus on the mother's left, over the fetal anterior shoulder
questions.why: The fetal heart is heard best through the fetal back, over the anterior shoulder. In a cephalic presentation this lies below the umbilicus, on the side of the fetal back.
notes: In a cephalic presentation the breech occupies the fundus, so the heart is too far away to hear well from here. This spot suits a breech presentation.
This is the side of the fetal limbs, and the area above the umbilicus is where the heart is heard in a breech presentation, not a cephalic one.
The head lies over the pelvic brim. The fetal heart is in the thorax, higher up and towards the side of the fetal back.
